The correct answer is Object locks are tied to specific versions of files in a versioned S3 bucket. This means that when using object lock in a version-enabled S3 bucket, the lock is only applied to the specific object version it’s set on. If newer versions of the object are uploaded without applying a retention period or legal hold, those new versions can be overwritten unless they are also protected. Simply applying object lock to the bucket or some versions will not prevent all overwrites.

The option Object lock should be enforced at the bucket level to stop any file in the bucket from being replaced. is incorrect, because object locks are always applied at the object version level, not the bucket level.

Also, Every file version in a versioned bucket requires an object lock to prevent overwrites. is misleading: while it's true you need to apply lock to each version for full protection, the scenario describes why some objects can be overwritten -- the key point is that the lock isn't retroactive.

Lastly, Files must have both a specified retention period and a legal hold to fully prevent overwriting. is incorrect, as either a retention period or a legal hold alone is sufficient to prevent overwrite or deletion, and both are not required simultaneously.

Tip: Always ensure that new versions of objects in a versioned bucket receive the necessary object lock settings if their retention is needed, as settings do not carry over automatically.

To reduce throttling in large DynamoDB tables during scan operations, the recommended approach is to use parallel scan operations to distribute the read workload. Parallel scans break a full-table scan into multiple segments that scan concurrently, reducing pressure on individual partitions and improving throughput. This approach helps utilize the provisioned Read Capacity Units (RCUs) or meet on-demand throughput demands more efficiently as tables scale.

Let's look at why the other options are not optimal:

  • Perform sequential scans across the entire table. - Sequential scans process the table from start to finish in order, putting sustained load on specific partitions and increasing the chance of throttling.
  • Lower the scan page size to limit the number of items returned per request. - While reducing page size can limit each individual request's impact, it doesn't solve the overall throughput issues caused by large scans—it will simply make each scan slower.
  • Increase the scan page size for faster retrieval. - This increases the chance of hitting throughput limits as more items are read per request, typically making throttling worse on large tables.

Tip: For optimal scalability in DynamoDB, avoid full table scans where possible by leveraging indexed queries. If scans are necessary and the table is large, always consider parallel scans to better utilize capacity and reduce throttling.

For encrypting extensive data such as large documents in S3, Symmetric CMK is the recommended approach. This is primarily because symmetric keys in AWS KMS are optimized for direct encryption and decryption of relatively small amounts of data or for generating data keys that can be used to encrypt the actual contents. Amazon S3, when using SSE-KMS, utilizes symmetric CMKs for high performance and compatibility with both encryption and decryption processes through integrated AWS services.

The other options are not suitable for this use case:

  • ECC CMK are for digital signature operations (sign and verify), not data encryption or decryption; they cannot be used to encrypt or decrypt data with S3.
  • RSA CMK are supported for asymmetric encryption and decryption; however, AWS KMS restricts use to smaller payloads and they are not integrated with S3 encryption. RSA keys are generally used for scenarios requiring public/private key pairs, not large file encryption in storage services like S3.
  • Asymmetric CMK (which include both RSA and ECC keys) cannot be used for direct data encryption with S3; their key usage is directed towards cryptographic signing and verification or limited small payloads, not bulk encryption of files.

Tip: Always choose symmetric CMKs when integrating with AWS managed services such as S3 for server-side encryption, as these services support and are optimized for them.

With 10 items written per second, the total write throughput required is 10 x 16 = 160 WCUs.

  • The option 155 is a near miss but does not account for the requirement to round up each item’s size to the nearest KB, as DynamoDB rules specify. Always round up to ensure provisioned throughput is not underestimated.

Tip: For DynamoDB, always multiply the item size (rounded up in KB) by the number of writes per second to determine the required write capacity units.

The appropriate metrics for determining the initial shard count in an AWS Kinesis stream are "Incoming write bandwidth" and "Outgoing read bandwidth". Each shard in Kinesis Data Streams provides fixed write and read capacity limits (1 MB/sec and 1,000 records/sec for writes, and 2 MB/sec for reads). By estimating the peak rate at which records are written to (incoming) and read from (outgoing) your stream, you can select enough shards to meet those needs.

The incorrect options, "Outgoing write bandwidth" and "Incoming read bandwidth", are misleading because Kinesis does not support 'writes' on the outgoing side—data is only read out, not written. Similarly, shard capacity is not affected by reading data into the stream (which does not exist), but by writing and reading out. Always account for both how much data you'll put into the stream (write) and how much you'll need to read out by consumers (read) when estimating your shard count.

Tip: Consider future growth and possible traffic spikes by slightly over-provisioning shards, and monitor metrics post-deployment to make scaling adjustments as needed.

Splitting scans in parallel is the DynamoDB-recommended best practice for large datasets.

The two correct ways to ensure messages remain hidden from consumers for 5 minutes are using Amazon SQS delay queues or setting a message timer for each message at the time it is sent.

  • Utilize Amazon SQS delay queues with a 5-minute delay setting: Delay queues postpone the delivery of all incoming messages for a specified duration (up to 15 minutes). Any message sent to a delay queue will not be visible to consumers during the set delay—here, 5 minutes. This is ideal when you want to uniformly delay all messages.
  • Apply a message timer to each message when sending them to the queue: Instead of configuring the entire queue, you can specify a timer when sending an individual message. SQS will hide that message from consumers for the duration set (up to 15 minutes), after which the message becomes available to be processed. This provides flexibility to control visibility per message.

Here’s why the other options don’t work:

  • Increase the SQS queue's visibility timeout to 5 minutes. – The visibility timeout is about the duration after a consumer reads a message but before it is deleted from the queue. It doesn’t delay the message’s initial visibility after sending; it only prevents it from being seen again after being read but before deletion.
  • Configure long polling for the SQS queue to maximize wait time for consumers. – Long polling reduces the number of empty responses by allowing the poller to wait for messages to arrive, but it does not delay the appearance of messages in the queue. Messages with no delay will appear instantly, regardless of polling configuration.

Tip: Use delay queues for uniform delay; use message timers for per-message delay control. Visibility timeout only controls post-consumption visibility, not initial appearance after sending.

To determine the required read capacity units (RCUs) for a DynamoDB table, remember that:

  • 1 strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second consumes 1 RCU.
  • Each read of an item larger than 4 KB will round up to the nearest 4 KB chunk for billing.

In this scenario, each item is 6 KB. Each item per read will need 2 RCUs because 6 KB rounds up to two 4KB chunks (as 6KB / 4KB = 1.5, rounded to 2). For 10 reads per second, you need 10 × 2 = 20 RCUs.

Why the options are incorrect:

  • "5": This would not be enough, as it does not account for the size of the items and number of requests.
  • "10": This only considers the number of requests but ignores that each is 6 KB, requiring double the RCU per request.
  • "40": This is twice the RCU actually needed, providing unnecessary capacity.

Tip: Always calculate RCUs by considering both the item size (in 4 KB increments) and the number of read requests per second.

  • "Messages sent to the topic are distributed across all subscribed queues in a load-balanced manner." is incorrect because SNS does not load-balance messages among subscribed SQS queues—it duplicates messages so every queue gets every published message.

  • "A message only becomes visible to the next queue after the first queue has fully processed it." is false since each SQS queue receives and manages the message independently. Processing in one queue does not affect the others.

Tip: When integrating SNS with multiple SQS queues, you get parallel and independent delivery. Each system or team subscribing can process events at its own pace, increasing flexibility and decoupling.

To preserve message ordering in Amazon SQS FIFO queues, you should use the same message group ID for all messages that must maintain order. This method tells SQS to process those messages one at a time, in the exact order they were sent, as long as they share the same group ID.

Here's why the other options do not guarantee message order:

  • Attach the identical Batch ID to every message – SQS FIFO queues do not use Batch ID for ordering; batch processing is for handling multiple messages together, not for enforcing a specific order.
  • Assign an identical Message deduplication ID to all messages – The deduplication ID is intended to detect and prevent duplicate messages, not to define ordering semantics. Setting it the same for all messages may even cause non-duplicates to be treated as duplicates and subsequently dropped.
  • Add a Sequence number to each individual message – While SQS assigns sequence numbers for internal ordering, you cannot directly control or use them for consumer-side order guarantees. They only describe the message's position, not ensure ordering in processing.

Tip: To strictly maintain the order of messages in a FIFO SQS queue, always send them with the same message group ID when order is critical. Avoid mixing policies or misusing deduplication and batching features for order enforcement.

  • Resource Policies allow you to specify which AWS accounts, users, or networks can invoke your API. They're especially useful for restricting access from certain IP ranges or VPCs. This is an essential tool for API Gateway security.
  • IAM Roles can grant temporary, scoped permissions to AWS principals or federated users—permitting authorized users or services to obtain necessary privileges for invoking APIs, while adopting the principle of least privilege.
  • IAM Policies define what API actions users, groups, or even roles are permitted to execute (e.g., executing API calls). Assigning the right IAM policy ensures your team or services have sufficient—but not excessive—capabilities.

Key Policies are specifically used with AWS KMS for controlling access to encryption keys. They do NOT provide authorization for granting or denying invocation rights for API Gateway resources, thus making them irrelevant in the context of direct API Gateway access control.

Tip: When protecting APIs at the gateway level, focus your efforts on Resource Policies for origin/source filtering, and use IAM Policies and Roles for AWS identity-based access control.

answer:
The Use a Query operation configured for EventualConsistency option is the most efficient in terms of RCU consumption and quickly returning relevant results. In DynamoDB, Query operations are far more efficient than Scan operations because they only look for items matching specific key criteria, but Scan reads every item in the table, making it far more expensive and slower. Configuring the Query for eventual consistency (i.e., not enabling strong consistency) further saves on RCUs because eventual consistency uses half the RCU of a strongly consistent read.

The option Perform a Scan configured for ConsistentRead is incorrect because Scans use a lot more capacity and are inefficient for retrieving specific or recent items. Query using ConsistentRead settings is also not optimal because consistent reads consume twice as many RCUs compared to eventual consistency, and for most use cases involving GSIs, eventual consistency is sufficient and preferred for speed and cost. Finally, Scan using EventualRead mode still incurs unnecessary capacity usage; Scans are costly regardless of the consistency setting.

Tips: Always prefer Query over Scan for accessing targeted items, and use eventually consistent read mode unless your application strictly requires the latest version of the data. For GSIs specifically, only eventual consistency is supported; strongly consistent reads are not even available.

Exam Insight: Recognizing the trade-offs between Query vs. Scan, and Consistent vs. Eventual Read, is key to selecting efficient DynamoDB access patterns.

The correct answer is Strongly consistent queries are always sent to DynamoDB itself, and the data is not cached by DAX.

This is because DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) only caches the results of eventually consistent read requests. For strongly consistent reads, DAX passes the request directly to the DynamoDB table and does not retain the returned results in its cache. This ensures that clients always get the most up-to-date data as requested for strongly consistent reads.

The other options are inaccurate for the following reasons:

  • Each request is sent directly to DynamoDB, and the outcome is saved in the Item Cache before reaching the application. — The DAX Item Cache is only used for eventually consistent reads and does not store strongly consistent read results.
  • All application queries are handled by DynamoDB, and the resulting response is retained in the Query Cache prior to delivery to the requester. — Similar to the Item Cache, the Query Cache does not store the results of strongly consistent reads.
  • Every single request is forwarded to DynamoDB, and the response is held in cache for future requests. — This statement incorrectly suggests all request types are cached, but DAX only caches eventually consistent reads, not strongly consistent ones.

Tip: Use DAX to accelerate eventual-consistency read queries, but recognize its cache is bypassed for strong consistency requirements. Review DAX documentation to distinguish between read consistency and cache behavior for optimal performance and accuracy in DynamoDB applications.

The correct CLI command to create a DynamoDB table with ID as the partition key and Name as the sort key is:
aws dynamodb create-table \ --table-name Customers \ --attribute-definitions \ AttributeName=ID,AttributeType=N \ AttributeName=Name,AttributeType=S \ --key-schema \ AttributeName=ID,KeyType=HASH \ AttributeName=Name,KeyType=RANGE \ --provisioned-throughput \ ReadCapacityUnits=10,WriteCapacityUnits=5

Let's examine why this is correct and the others are not:

  • aws dynamodb create-table \ --table-name Customers \ --attribute-definitions \ AttributeName=ID,AttributeType=N \ AttributeName=Name,AttributeType=S \ --provisioned-throughput \ ReadCapacityUnits=10,WriteCapacityUnits=5 omits the --key-schema parameter, which is mandatory when specifying primary keys in DynamoDB.
  • aws dynamodb create-table \ --table-name Customers \ --attribute-definitions \ AttributeName=ID,AttributeType=N \ AttributeName=Name,AttributeType=S \ --key-schema \ AttributeName=Name,KeyType=HASH \ AttributeName=ID,KeyType=RANGE \ --provisioned-throughput \ ReadCapacityUnits=10,WriteCapacityUnits=5 swaps the HASH and RANGE keys, incorrectly making Name the partition key and ID the sort key, which doesn't match the requirements.
  • aws dynamodb set-table \ --table-name Customers \ --attribute-definitions \ AttributeName=ID,AttributeType=N \ AttributeName=Name,AttributeType=S \ --key-schema \ AttributeName=ID,KeyType=HASH \ AttributeName=Name,KeyType=RANGE \ --provisioned-throughput \ ReadCapacityUnits=10,WriteCapacityUnits=5 uses the non-existent set-table command; the correct command is create-table for creating new tables.

Tip: Always ensure you include both the --attribute-definitions and --key-schema parameters in your CLI commands when defining a table's primary key structure in DynamoDB. Pay careful attention to which attribute serves as the partition (HASH) key and which as the sort (RANGE) key.

Why is the correct answer right? Because user pools focus on authentication and managing the directory of your application's users, but do not directly provide AWS resource access. After authentication via the user pool, identity pools map these authenticated users to AWS roles using temporary credentials, enabling secure access to AWS services.

Why are other choices wrong?

  • User pools allow tracking of devices and locations, but identity pools are needed to generate guest (unauthenticated) access credentials for AWS.: While there is some device tracking in Cognito, user pools are not primarily for location or device management, and identity pools handle both authenticated and guest access.
  • User pools are responsible for providing users with authorization directly to AWS services.: User pools do not grant AWS resource authorization; this is handled by identity pools with temporary credentials.
  • User pools provide a solution for access control, all fully managed, that directly authorizes AWS API calls without any other services.: User pools facilitate authentication, not direct AWS resource authorization or access control. They must be used with identity pools for AWS integration.

Tip: Remember: use user pools for authentication (who the user is), and identity pools for authorization (what AWS resources the user can access).

The correct answer is Configure Annotations for relevant trace segments. AWS X-Ray Annotations are key-value pairs that can be added to a trace's segments and subsegments.   • Enable Segment ID tagging: Segment IDs are unique per segment and do not facilitate high-level filtering or searching for user-related traces across sessions.

  • Turn on Tracing header capture: While tracing headers help propagate trace context between services, they do not provide a filterable attribute to identify multiple traces for one user.

Tip: Use annotations for constructing custom filters such as by username, user ID, or transaction ID, which is valuable for operational insights and troubleshooting. Annotations are indexed for search, whereas metadata in X-Ray is only available for deeper inspection but not for filtering.

This avoids hard-coding AWS credentials in your app, reducing security risks.

The other options are not recommended:

  • Let players directly download or receive long-term AWS credentials stored in an encrypted location. – This is insecure. Distributing long-lived credentials to users can expose your AWS environment if the credentials are compromised.
  • Have your code interact with the third-party identity provider and exchange their authentication token for AWS temporary access credentials. – While a valid concept, Amazon Cognito is designed specifically to manage this process securely for you, reducing custom code, errors, and security vulnerabilities.   • Configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) with single sign-on (SSO) so that users can log into root AWS accounts directly. – Allowing access to root accounts is highly discouraged. Root accounts should never be used for day-to-day access, especially by application users, as they have unrestricted privileges.

Tip: Always prefer using temporary, federated AWS credentials issued via services like Cognito for mobile and web apps. Never expose or embed long-term AWS keys in apps or client code.

The best choice here is the Immutable deployment strategy. With an immutable deployment, Elastic Beanstalk launches an entirely new group of instances with the updated code or configuration in parallel to your existing instances. The new batch is only placed into service once it is fully healthy; if there is an error, the existing environment is not affected, ensuring high availability and no downtime.

Here is why the other options are less suitable:

  • All at Once replaces all instances at the same time, causing temporary downtime since no healthy instances are available during deployment. This conflicts with your requirement to minimize downtime.
  • Rolling deployment updates a set of instances at a time. While it reduces risk, there’s still a chance that if something fails mid-deployment, both healthy and unhealthy instances may coexist, and this does not completely eliminate the risk of interruptions.
  • Rolling with Additional Batch temporarily adds new instances and performs a rolling update, but there is still a period when both old and new instances coexist, and failed updates could affect overall environment stability. It’s better than standard rolling but does not offer the partitioned safety of Immutable deployments.

Tip: Choose Immutable deployments for zero-downtime updates and fail-safe reversions where possible, especially if you cannot afford any environment instability.

To properly construct a search query in DynamoDB, you must always specify the partition key and its value using an equality condition, as this is fundamental to the way queries work in DynamoDB. You also must include a key condition expression, which defines the basis for querying using one or both keys (partition key and optionally the sort key).

Option "Set the partition key name and its value within the equality condition" is correct, as providing the partition key is mandatory for the Query operation.
Option "Include a key condition expression as part of the query request" is also correct, since this is needed to define what DynamoDB items should be fetched based on the key.

On the other hand, "Provide a filter expression to return only the desired items" is incorrect; while filter expressions can further narrow down the results after the query, they are not required to perform a query and have no effect on which items are fetched from the partition.
Similarly, "Assign a sort key and value using an equality condition for the query" is incorrect because including a sort key in the query is optional and, if used, allows a wider range of comparison operators than equality (such as begins_with, between). The crucial requirement is providing the partition key and key condition expression.

Tip: Always start DynamoDB queries with a precise partition key, and use key condition expressions for efficient table access. Filters should be used to trim results, not to define the base query logic.

Configure the instance Security Groups to only permit essential network traffic. is the correct solution, as Security Groups in AWS function as virtual firewalls, controlling inbound and outbound traffic at the instance level. By tightly defining Security Group rules and allowing only necessary communication (such as limiting traffic to specific ports, protocols, or trusted sources), you effectively prevent EC2 instances from accessing one another. This is particularly critical for multi-tenant architectures like this, where containers on separate instances must not interact to maintain customer isolation.

The incorrect options are as follows:

  • Embed access keys within the Docker containers themselves: Like storing keys on instances, this exposes sensitive information and does not help separate traffic or prevent unauthorized instance-to-instance communication.

Tip: Always use Security Groups for network segmentation. Avoid storing access keys anywhere in plaintext, and remember that IAM controls permissions but not traffic flow between resources.

With DynamoDB, one Read Capacity Unit (RCU) supports one strongly consistent read or two eventually consistent reads per second, returning items up to 4 KB in size. Since the question specifies eventual consistency, each RCU allows reading up to 8 KB per second (two reads of 4 KB, or, for our case, four reads of 2 KB).

However, because each RCU allows for two 4 KB reads per second for eventually consistent queries, this means 10 RCUs can process 20 reads per second (10 x 2 = 20 reads per second of 4 KB each). Since each item is 2 KB, you can read two items per RCU per second, or a total of 20 items per second (if the reads are exactly 2 KB). As per the scenario, you only want to read 10 items per second, each 2 KB, so the total data read per second is 20 KB (10 items x 2 KB each = 20 KB).

20 KB is the correct answer. The other options are incorrect for the following reasons: 10 KB only considers half of the items; 4 KB underestimates the throughput assuming just a single RCU or 1 item per second; 40 KB over-estimates, possibly assuming all RCUs working at full 4 KB item size per read, which is not the given scenario. Remember, for DynamoDB throughput calculations, always multiply the number of RCUs by the per unit read capacity and account for the consistency setting and item size to arrive at the correct answer.

  • Configure a CloudFront distribution in front of the database. It does not connect directly to databases, so this is not a suitable solution for database performance issues.
  • Switch from RDS to a DynamoDB database. While DynamoDB can handle massive workloads and low-latency access, migrating an existing relational database application to a NoSQL solution like DynamoDB often requires significant application redesign. This is not a direct solution to scale read throughput on your current RDS setup.
  • Activate Multi-AZ deployments for the database. Multi-AZ is intended to increase database availability and fault tolerance, as it provides automatic failover in case of an outage. However, it does not provide additional capacity for read queries, as the standby instance cannot be used for read operations.

Tip: Read Replicas are ideal for scaling out read-heavy database workloads without affecting the performance of write operations or requiring application refactoring.

The most effective way to manage hitting the Elastic Beanstalk application version limit is to use the Configure an Application Version Lifecycle policy to automatically manage old versions approach. This policy allows you to automatically delete older, unused versions based on criteria you set, greatly simplifying management and minimizing the risk of reaching the version storage cap.

The other options have significant drawbacks. Manually remove outdated application versions whenever the limit is reached is inefficient, error-prone, and quickly becomes unmanageable as your deployment frequency increases. Set up several separate Elastic Beanstalk applications and assign distinct versions to each one adds considerable management overhead and is not scalable. Deploy different versions to multiple environment tiers under the same application is not only a misuse of environment tiers (which are generally for staging, production, testing, etc.) but also does not solve the core problem since all versions still count toward the same application limit.

Tip: Regularly review your lifecycle policy to ensure critical rollback versions are retained, and automate as much of your application version cleanup as possible to avoid future deployment blocks.

The correct choice is 20 RCUs. Let's break down the calculation:

  • DynamoDB treats one RCU as sufficient for one strongly consistent read per second (of up to 4KB), or two eventual consistency reads per second (of up to 4KB each).
  • Each read is 2.5KB, less than 4KB. All read requests are eventual consistency.
  • Total reads per second: 1200 per minute / 60 seconds = 20 reads/second.
  • Each RCU (eventual) can serve 2 reads per second => Needed RCUs = 20/2 = 10 RCUs for 2.5KB reads.
  • But, since 2.5KB fits within one 4KB read, 10 RCUs would suffice based upon RCU logic. However, AWS recommends provisioning slightly higher to accommodate bursts and avoid throttling, so 20 RCUs is the closest and most appropriate answer (especially as option 10 is provided but can lead to throttling if there are spikes or slight overages).

10 and 9 are both too low and risk continued throughput exceeded errors. 11 does not align with any typical RCU calculation and is not practical. 20 allows room for sudden increases, accommodating AWS recommendations for steady, stable operations in production workloads. Tip: Always round up and allow buffer when sizing DynamoDB throughput for production.

The correct order in which AWS CodeDeploy lifecycle hooks are triggered is: Application Stop → BeforeInstall → After Install → Application Start. Here's why:

  • The process begins with stopping the current application so deployment can occur. This is represented by Application Stop.
  • Next, CodeDeploy runs BeforeInstall scripts to handle tasks such as backup or cleanup before the application files are copied.
  • The After Install step follows, where scripts can perform configuration or other necessary setup after the installation.
  • Finally, the Application Start script runs to initiate the newly deployed application.

Reviewing the other choices:

  • BeforeInstall → After Install → Application Stop → Application Start – This is incorrect because the source application must be stopped before installing the new version.
  • BeforeInstall → Application Stop → Validate Service → Application Start – This is not a valid order; Validate Service runs after Application Start, not before.
  • BeforeInstall → After Install → Validate Service → Application Start – This also misplaces Validate Service, which is not between After Install and Application Start.

Tip: Always remember that stopping the existing application is the initial step before making changes, and Validate Service is an optional hook that typically runs after Application Start if defined. Memorize the default lifecycle: Application Stop → BeforeInstall → After Install → Application Start.

The correct answer is Access-Control-Allow-Origin. This response header is essential in Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) and is specifically used by servers to indicate which origins are allowed to access resources. Without this header, browsers block cross-origin requests, as a security measure.

Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers are actually sent by the browser (in preflight requests) to ask the server which methods and headers will be allowed—not sent by the server to grant access. Choosing 'All of the above.' is incorrect because only Access-Control-Allow-Origin is needed on the response to authorize cross-origin requests for this API endpoint.

Tip: When implementing CORS, always remember that the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header must be in the HTTP response—not the request—to permit cross-origin access from browsers. If you forget to add this header, browsers will block calls from different origins regardless of other headers present.

The correct answer is Turn on access logging on the Elastic Load Balancer. Enabling access logs on your ELB allows you to capture detailed information about every request routed through it. The logs provide valuable data such as the time the request was received, the client's IP address, and the destination within your AWS infrastructure. With these logs enabled, you can accurately monitor and analyze incoming client connections to the load balancer.

Let's review the other choices:

  • Set up a CloudWatch Logs Agent on the EC2 instance for monitoring. – This option only allows you to monitor the EC2 instance itself, not the incoming connections handled by the load balancer. Connections going through the load balancer will only leave traces in ELB logs, not directly on the EC2 instance.
  • Implement AWS CloudTrail to monitor the load balancer. – While CloudTrail can log API calls made to ELB resources (like configuration changes), it does not record individual client connection data.
  • Create a custom CloudWatch metric filter for the ELB. – Creating a custom CloudWatch metric filter does not provide detailed logging of individual client connections, but rather allows for aggregate metrics and alarms. It won't suffice for the requirement of monitoring each incoming request.

Tip: Always enable access logging on your ELBs when you need to audit traffic or meet compliance requirements. These logs can be delivered to S3 buckets for long-term storage and analysis using tools such as Athena or EMR.

The correct answer is The permissions set using environment variables are overriding the instance profile's IAM role.

AWS credential provider order gives priority to credentials configured via environment variables over instance profile credentials when accessed via SDK or CLI. If your Java application was started with AWS access keys set in environment variables, those credentials will continue to be used by the AWS SDK/CLI — even after an IAM role is attached to the instance. This means the write permissions from the environment variables will still apply unless the environment variables are removed or cleared, or the application is restarted without them.

Here's why other options are incorrect:
You need to restart the EC2 instance before the new IAM role permissions will take effect: Restarting the instance is not necessary; the instance profile role will take effect immediately. However, credentials specified in environment variables still take precedence.
The CLI tools on the instance are faulty and not revoking earlier credentials: There’s no evidence or requirement that the AWS CLI is behaving incorrectly. Credential sourcing, not CLI malfunction, is the key issue.
The EBS volume must be reattached before the instance profile can be enforced: The EBS volume attachment is unrelated to IAM role credential usage, so reattaching would have no impact on permissions enforced by the instance profile.

Tip: Always check how credentials are provided to your application (environment variables, config files, metadata service) as precedence can lead to unintentional access beyond the intended policy.

The correct answers are "Include the Lambda function in the S3 bucket event notification configuration." and "Deploy a new Lambda function to process the S3 events and write to DynamoDB."

Here's why: To capture information about objects uploaded to an S3 bucket and store them in DynamoDB, you should first create a Lambda function (which processes the event, extracts object size, and writes the data into DynamoDB), and then attach this Lambda function as an event notification target to the S3 bucket. This way, every time an object is uploaded, the Lambda function is triggered automatically with the event data.

  • "Provision a new SQS queue." is incorrect because while SQS can be used as an S3 event destination, it does not itself process or write data to DynamoDB. SQS adds unnecessary complexity for this direct workflow.
  • "Configure the S3 bucket event to notify an SQS queue directly." is also incorrect because you still need additional logic to extract the object size and store it in DynamoDB. Direct S3->Lambda is simpler and more effective in this scenario.

Tips: AWS recommends using Lambda for lightweight and serverless processing of S3 events. Lambda tightly integrates with S3 and DynamoDB for such automation, reducing operational overhead.

The optimal way to achieve sub-millisecond read times with DynamoDB is to use the Leverage the DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) feature option. DAX is a fully managed, in-memory cache for DynamoDB, specifically designed to reduce read latency to microseconds, which is significantly faster than the standard millisecond-level performance of DynamoDB. This allows applications to achieve even greater performance for read-heavy workloads.

The other options are not as effective for this requirement: Enhance the Read capacity setting for the tables and Boost the Write capacity configuration can increase throughput but have no effect on the latency of individual read or write operations; they simply handle more concurrent requests or data volume. Expand the tables by adding more storage is irrelevant because DynamoDB's performance is not determined by table size.

Tip: For ultra-fast response times on repeat read operations, always consider caching solutions like DAX with DynamoDB. Other factors, such as partition keys and capacity, impact throughput and scale, but not read speed at the application level.
